data.text: Now that you understand the project structure, it is time to build a **real endpoint**. In this lesson you will create a small `UsersController` that exposes the full CRUD surface — list, read one, create, update, and delete — using only an in-memory list.
You will learn how routing attributes map URLs to C# methods, how `[ApiController]` enables automatic model validation, and how to return the right `IActionResult` for each scenario.

terms.definition: A class that groups related HTTP endpoints. Inherits from `ControllerBase` (for APIs) or `Controller` (for MVC views).
A public method on a controller that handles a specific HTTP request.
Routing driven by attributes like `[Route]`, `[HttpGet]`, `[HttpPost]` rather than a centralized route table.
The return type that lets an action send any HTTP response (200, 404, 400, etc.) from a single method.
Attribute that enables opinionated defaults: automatic 400 responses, binding source inference, problem details for errors.

data.text: Define a simple `User` record to represent our resource. Records give us value-based equality and a clean constructor for free — perfect for DTO-shaped types.

data.title: Models/User.cs
data.content: A minimal record representing a user.
data.code:
namespace MyWebApi.Models;

public record User(int Id, string Name, string Email);

data.title: Records vs classes
data.text: Use a **record** for immutable DTOs and a regular **class** when you need mutable state, inheritance, or EF Core entity behavior.

Add a new file at `Controllers/UsersController.cs`. The `[ApiController]` attribute turns on the standard API conventions; `[Route]` sets the URL prefix, and `[HttpGet]` / `[HttpPost]` map individual methods to HTTP verbs.

data.title: Controllers/UsersController.cs
data.content: Full CRUD controller with five endpoints and correct `using` directives.

data.title: Fixes applied to the snippet
data.text: Compared to a naive first draft, the code above adds the `MyWebApi.Models` namespace, renames the parameterless `Get` to `GetAll` to avoid overload resolution issues, and adds the `[FromBody]` attribute on `Create` so the JSON body binds correctly.

ASP.NET Core combines the controller-level `[Route]` template with each action's HTTP-method attribute to build the final URL. The literal `[controller]` token is replaced with the controller class name **minus** the `Controller` suffix.

data.caption: How `[Route]`, `[HttpGet]`, and `[controller]` combine into a URL.
data.definition:
flowchart TB
    A[Class: UsersController] -->|"[controller]"| C[users]
    B["[Route('api/[controller]')]"] --> D[api/users]
    E["[HttpGet]"] --> F[/]
    G["[HttpGet('{id:int}')]"] --> H[/{id:int}]
    D --> I[Final URL template]
    C --> I
    F --> I
    H --> I

terms.definition: A route constraint — matches only integer values. `/api/users/abc` returns 404 instead of a binding error.
Tells the binder to deserialize the request body (JSON by default) into the parameter.
Returns 201 with a `Location` header pointing at the URL of the newly created resource.

data.text: Action Results You Will Use Daily

data.title: Pick the right result for the situation

cards.title: Ok(data)
cards.description: Returns `200 OK` with an optional body.
pros: Standard for successful reads and updates
cons: Not appropriate for 'created' — use `CreatedAtAction` instead so the client gets a Location header

cards.title: CreatedAtAction(...)
cards.description: Returns `201 Created` with a `Location` header pointing at the new resource.
pros: Signals that a new resource was created
Gives clients a stable URL for the new resource
cons: Requires you to know the action name and route parameter names

cards.title: NotFound()
cards.description: Returns `404 Not Found` with no body.
pros: Trivially indicates 'the resource you asked for is not there'
cons: Empty body — consider `Problem(...)` for a richer error message

cards.title: NoContent()
cards.description: Returns `204 No Content` with no body.
pros: Idiomatic for successful DELETE when there is nothing meaningful to return
cons: Do not use if you need to confirm what was deleted — return `Ok` instead

cards.title: BadRequest() / ValidationProblem()
cards.description: Returns `400 Bad Request` with optional error details.
cons: You rarely need to call it manually

data.title: ActionResult<T> vs IActionResult
data.text: Prefer `ActionResult<T>` on actions so the **Swagger/OpenAPI generator** knows the success type. `IActionResult` alone leaves the response shape unknown to tooling.

items.hint: Not `Controller` — that adds view support you do not need in an API.

items.text: Every action method is decorated with an HTTP-method attribute.

items.hint: Without it, the binder may try to read from the query string.

items.text: The class has `[ApiController]` and a `[Route]` attribute.
items.hint: Otherwise, automatic 400 responses will not kick in.

data.title: Extend the controller
data.description: Practice the patterns you just learned by adding a small enhancement to the controller.
steps: Add a `[HttpGet("search")]` action that returns users filtered by a `name` query string parameter (case-insensitive `Contains`).
Return `404 Not Found` when no users match.
Use the `MyWebApi.http` file (or Postman) to POST a user, then GET `/api/users/search?name=<your substring>` to verify.
Add a `Count` field to the `User` record (or remove it if you prefer) and confirm the controller still compiles and runs.
data.expectedOutcome: A new `/api/users/search?name=...` endpoint that returns the filtered list (or 404 if none), and a working confirmation flow in your HTTP client of choice.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Controllers inherit `ControllerBase` and are decorated with `[ApiController]` and `[Route]`.
HTTP-method attributes (`[HttpGet]`, `[HttpPost]`, ...) map actions to verbs; `[FromBody]` tells the binder to use JSON.
Return `ActionResult<T>` so OpenAPI tooling knows the response shape.
Use `Ok`, `CreatedAtAction`, `NoContent`, and `NotFound` to communicate the right status code for each outcome.
Route constraints like `{id:int}` keep invalid input from reaching your action.
data.takeaway: Controllers are the bridge between HTTP and C#. Master the attributes, return the right status codes, and the rest is regular C# code.
